text: You walk into a room, and forget why you came in.
It's not your memory failing. It's the door.
In 2011, psychologist Gabriel Radvansky, at the University of Notre Dame, ran a simple test.
People carried objects from one table to another, room after room.
Some walked through a doorway. Others walked the same distance, with no door at all.
The ones who crossed a doorway forgot more.
Your brain doesn't record life like a film. It cuts it into scenes.
A doorway tells it the scene is over. File the old one. Start fresh.
Psychologists call it an event boundary.
Most people think it's a glitch. It's a tool.
Before you walk through a door, say what you came for. Out loud.
Carry it across the line on purpose.
And the thought you can't put down tonight?
Leave it on the other side of a door. Walk out. Let the scene end.
Every room you enter, your brain asks one question.
So what did you leave in the last room?
